office.title: Indiana State Representative
office.summary: Members of the Indiana House of Representatives write and vote on state laws as part of the Indiana General Assembly. The House has 100 members, each representing one district for a two-year term [1].
duties: Introduces and votes on state legislation as one of the two chambers of the Indiana General Assembly [1].
Must be at least 21 years old when taking office and have lived in the district for at least a year [1].

incumbent.name: Chris Jeter
incumbent.summary: Chris Jeter, a Fishers Republican and attorney, has represented House District 88 since August 2020 and chairs the House Judiciary Committee [3]. He is a Navy Reserve officer and a partner at a Fishers law firm [3].
record: Committees: Judiciary (chair); Courts and Criminal Code; Utilities, Energy and Telecommunications [3]. His campaign says he co-chairs the state's Bail and Release Review Commission [4]. In June 2026 he was named chair of the Interim Study Committee on Courts and the Judiciary, according to the caucus [3].
Feb. 2024: The House passed his bills to add funding for deputy prosecutors and to create two new superior courts and two magistrate positions in Hamilton County, according to the caucus [3].

April 10, 2025: Voted yes on SEA 1, the 2025 property-tax law (passed 65-29) [5]. April 25, 2025: Voted yes on HEA 1001, the 2025-27 budget (adopted 66-27) [6]. Dec. 5, 2025: Recorded as excused on HB 1032, the mid-decade congressional redistricting bill, which passed the House 57-41 [7].

2026 session: After the death of Fishers teen Hailey Buzbee, Jeter highlighted an amendment to HB 1303 expanding the definition of a missing child to include a "high-risk missing person" [8]. He also highlighted HEA 1408, which the caucus says requires parental consent for minors' social media accounts [9]. Voted yes on HB 1002, the utility-affordability bill, on Jan. 28, 2026 [10].

race_context: House District 88 includes portions of Hamilton, Hancock, Madison and Marion counties [3]. Yocum's campaign lists the Geist area of Indianapolis, part of Lawrence, McCordsville, Fortville, Mt. Comfort, Ingalls and part of Fishers [11].
This is a rematch: Yocum was the 2024 Democratic nominee, and Jeter won that year with 57.8% [12]. In 2022 Jeter won 60% to 40% over Democrat Donna Griffin [13].
May 5, 2026 primaries: Wikipedia's 2026 election page lists Jeter as the only declared Republican and Yocum as the only declared Democrat [12].
No debate or forum between the candidates was found.

Key differences: Jeter points to income-tax cuts, the 2025 property-tax law and the 2026 utility law as his affordability record [14]. Yocum says the legislature has "diverted more and more funding away from public schools" and has overridden local decisions on data centers, schools and community planning [15].

candidates.summary: Republican incumbent since 2020 and chair of the House Judiciary Committee [3]. In 2026 columns he has emphasized affordability, Healthy Indiana Plan work requirements and girls' sports rules [14, 16, 17].
background: Attorney; partner at Massillamany Jeter & Carson LLP in Fishers, which he co-founded in 2015; J.D. from George Washington University and bachelor's degree from Oklahoma Baptist University [3].
Served seven years on active duty as a Navy JAG officer, including as a Special Assistant U.S. Attorney, and is now a Navy Reserve officer [3, 4].
Serves on the Fishers Economic Development Commission; lives in Fishers [3].
path_to_ballot: Selected in 2020 to fill the District 88 seat and reelected since [4]. Listed as the only declared Republican in the May 5, 2026 primary [12].

items: Says he supported cutting the state income tax rate from 3.15% in 2023 to 2.95%, with a cut to 2.9% scheduled for 2027 [14]. Says "if government can responsibly leave another dollar in the pocket of a Hoosier family, we should look for a way to do it" [14].
Supported SEA 1 (2025), which he describes as projected to save homeowners $1.3 billion over three years; says "We need to keep driving down property taxes" [14, 5].
Says he supported HEA 1001 (2026) because it "takes aim at unnecessary local barriers that can restrict housing supply and drive up construction costs" [18].
Cites his 2022 vote to eliminate the utility receipts tax and his support for HEA 1002 (2026), which he says "holds utilities accountable for affordability" [18, 10].

Supports the 2026 law requiring able-bodied Healthy Indiana Plan enrollees to complete 80 hours a month of work, job training, education or community service starting Jan. 1, 2027, with exemptions; wrote that "a safety net should never become a hammock" [16].

Said the HB 1303 missing-child amendment is "part of a much larger effort to modernize Indiana's child welfare and endangerment laws" [8]. Said of HEA 1408, "Parents deserve greater confidence that their children are protected online" [9].

Co-authored HEA 1041 (2022), which he describes as protecting girls competing in K-12 athletics, and voted to override the governor's veto of it; wrote in August 2026 that "protecting a separate category for female athletics should not require courage in 2026" [17].

on_incumbent: Is the current officeholder. No statements by Jeter about his 2026 challenger were found.
plans: Says Indiana should "continue cutting taxes when fiscally responsible, control property taxes, expand housing supply, demand reliable and affordable energy, confront healthcare costs and remove unnecessary barriers to economic growth" [18].
endorsements_finance: No endorsements or 2026 fundraising totals were found in the sources reviewed.
gaps: No reason was found for his excused absence on the HB 1032 redistricting vote, and no public statement of his position on that bill was found.
Whether the 2024 deputy-prosecutor and Hamilton County court bills became law was not verified.
Whether he authored (rather than supported) HEA 1408 was not verified.
Campaign finance reports were not reviewed.

candidates.summary: Democratic nominee and 2024 nominee for this seat; nonprofit executive who chairs Serve Indiana, the governor-appointed state service commission [19, 12]. Her platform centers on public schools, affordability and local control [15].
background: Vice president at a large nonprofit focused on education and young children's well-being; more than 20 years in nonprofit leadership in education and health care; former AmeriCorps member [19].
Chairs Serve Indiana, the governor-appointed Commission on Service and Volunteerism [19].
Graduated from Marion High School and attended Hanover College [19]. Her campaign lists a McCordsville mailing address [11].
path_to_ballot: Was the Democratic nominee in 2024 and lost to Jeter [12]. Listed as the only declared Democrat in the May 5, 2026 primary [12].

items: Says "our state legislature has diverted more and more funding away from public schools"; pledges to "Fully fund public schools," support and retain teachers, ensure transparency in education spending and protect local school board decisions [15].

Pledges to expand access to affordable child care, support housing for families, young professionals and seniors, ensure "responsible budgeting and transparent spending," and support small businesses [15].

Says the legislature has been "overriding decisions about development (like data centers), schools, judicial appointments, and community planning"; pledges to "Restore decision-making authority to local governments" [15].

on_incumbent: Her 2026 site says she "can't stand by and watch political extremism make life harder for Indiana families" but does not name Jeter [11]. In her 2024 campaign, she said, "Our current Representative [State Rep. Chris Jeter] represents the most extreme in politics," and said she wanted to break the Republican supermajority [20].
plans: Says she will "focus on practical, common-sense solutions that strengthen our communities, lower costs for families, and put people ahead of politics" [15].
endorsements_finance: In 2024, Indianapolis City-County Councilor Nick Roberts endorsed her at her campaign kickoff [20]. No 2026 endorsements or fundraising totals were found.
gaps: Unverified (search snippets only; Current Publishing returned 403): a Jan. 13, 2026 Current article on her filing, which reportedly described the district as including parts of Fishers, Geist, Lawrence, McCordsville, Fortville and Madison County.
Little 2026 news coverage of her campaign was found.
Her 2024 positions on reproductive rights and the Second Amendment (reported in 2024) are not repeated on her current issues page and are not listed here as 2026 positions.
Campaign finance reports were not reviewed.
